utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. Mr. Registrar, please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Can I have the appearances, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Ken Scott for the Prosecutor, together with Daryl Mundis, Roeland Bos, and Skye Winner. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Defence counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Michael Karnavas for Dr. Jadranko Prlic, along with Suzana Tomanovic, co-counsel, and Ana Vlahovic, legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Senka Nozica on behalf of Bruno Stojic, assisted by Valent Slonje, our case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Bozidar Kovacic. I represent Mr. Praljak, and I'm assisted by Nika Pinter. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Vesna Alaburic. I represent Milivoj Petkovic, and Davor Lazic is my case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Tomislav Jonjic. I represent Mr. Valentin Coric and I'm assisted by Krystyna Grinberg, legal assistant, and Ida Jurkovic, case manager.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Pusic, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, Roger Sahota, and our legal assistant, Nermin Mulalic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On behalf of the Trial Chamber, I greet everybody here in the courtroom; the accused, the Prosecution, the Defence counsel, and all the people helping us. As you know, today we are going to start with a new witness. The testimony will continue tomorrow. But we have to finish our day at 4.00 because there is a Status Conference scheduled at 4.30 with Judge Meron. So we will have to leave this courtroom at 4.00. And we might have to have shorter breaks, slightly shorter breaks. We'll have 15 instead of 20 minutes. And as to the lunch break, it will not be 60 minutes but 50 minutes. This being said, let me tackle two other logistical matters. Yesterday I noted that when a party asked for a document to be submitted to the witness, it took some time before you could see the document on the screen. I discussed this with the Registrar, who told me that, generally speaking, it takes some 10 to 15 seconds for the document to appear, or even 30 seconds. But last night I did a calculation. If we are to tender into evidence over 10.000 documents, multiplied by this number of seconds, this is going to turn into hours if not days. So we're going to proceed with the system, but if we ever were to see that it takes too much time, I think that it's better to move back to the old system where we straight away have the document on the overhead projector, and it takes hardly a few seconds. I will see. I mean, no problem when it's about some hundred documents, but here, I mean, we have a huge amount of documents. Look at yesterday's hearing. The Defence, as I saw, had several documents for their cross-examination. So I can expect to be snowed under by documents from the Defence. So we'll have to take this into account. Second problem: During cross-examination, if you want to submit a document, well, as Judges we do not presently know whether the document you are about to submit was disclosed to you by the Prosecution, documents you are then about to use, or whether it is a document that you found yourself after looking for it and that you would have told the Prosecutor 20 hours before and you had sort of submitted to the Registry. So whenever you have a document, please tell us about its origin. Was it provided by the Prosecution or not? If it is a document you have found, tell us where it comes from, whether it comes from archives or not. Just for saving time. You know that I want to be very fast when it comes to the admissibility of documents. It's up to you later on should there be a challenge. In the end, through filings later, you could ask for it to be withdrawn. But to save time, there's no problem when it comes to admitting just about immediately a document. But to make our work easier, just tell us where it comes from. Most of the time I check whether there are stamps or signatures. However, there again if you give us a document that I haven't seen before, in a matter of seconds I have to check all this because the document is right away submitted to the witness. So as much as possible tell us where the document comes from in order to save time. A last minor item before the witness comes in: I know that some time ago a wish was expressed for the accused to have laptops which they could use to key in information during the hearing. I know that this is some of your concern, Mr. Karnavas. I am sure that you're going to tackle this straight away, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I am. Again good morning, Mr. President and Your Honours. In fact, I do have a laptop for my client. The idea was that we would bring it in every day for Mr. Prlic to use. At the end of the day, he would burn the CD of what he had typed so he could take it and download it in the computer that is provided to him at the UNDU. We would take the computer back, the laptop back every day. That way there is no security risk whatsoever. Then Mr. Prlic, if he has any notes from the night before, he would bring the CD, we would then download that material and that way we could have his input since we don't have e-mail. Now, in the event that that's not workable, or in the alternative I would say, and something that I would prefer, actually, is to have my client sitting next to me. You alluded to that, Mr. President. I think that this is a mature enough institution, and now that we have the system -- the courtroom redesigned, there is no reason why Mr. Prlic can't be sitting next to me, I can have direct access to the client. This is done all over the United States with -- irrespective of the crime charged, and I don't see the security risk. Now, I haven't spoken with security. I suspect that others would do, but they're there by the doors, and so I don't see a problem. Others may. But in any event, I would certainly request that that matter be looked into and, if possible, to have our client sitting next to us so we can have their full input throughout the trial. Yesterday, I believe Mr. Prlic wanted to pass me a note. He had to give it to a guard. Thankfully, the legal assistant for one of the teams brought it over. This cannot be done, especially when we're going to have some pretty important witnesses where the clients have a great deal of knowledge, inside knowledge, that we don't have even though we've had access to our clients for the last year or so. In any event, I would most appreciate it if you could look into this, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Wait a minute. Wait a minute. I'm going to give you the floor, Mr. Scott. Mr. Kovacic, on this same item?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to say something about what you said about presenting documents with regard to providing information on the source of the documents. That's not a problem at all, naturally. We'll always be in a position to identify the document since it's a document we obtained from our own databases, and as a result, we know the source of these documents. However, I'm somewhat concerned by you mentioning that we should provide the Prosecution with documents 20 hours in advance. As far as the technical procedure is concerned, I think that sometimes it will be impossible to do this. I have to tell you how we work to explain my position. Today we will be hearing a witness, and let's say we finish hearing the witness by the end of the day. It's not until this evening that we'll be able to examine his testimony, although we have a folder containing documents that might be interesting with regard to that witness. But it's only this evening that we'll know the nature of his testimony in the course of the examination-in-chief and only then we'll be able to decide on the nature of the cross-examination. So it won't be until 10.00, 11.00, 12.00 at night that we can decide which documents we'll be selecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry for interrupting you. I just thought of something. You said "the witness." Does that mean that the Prosecution witness is going to be seen by you before he or she comes into this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. But we first prepare ourselves on the basis of his previously given statements, the statements that the witness has usually given to the Prosecution or to other services, and then we have a rough selection of documents, documents of a general nature. But it's only after we have heard the witness in the courtroom, after we have seen what the nature of the examination-in-chief is that we can decide which specific documents to select, and this is done at night, in the evening. So we barely have enough time to do this because there are certain procedures that we have to follow in the e-court. If we've already inputted these documents in the e-court, that's not a problem; but if not, it is. So it's only before the hearing is held that we can decide on the documents to use. And I don't want my right to use a certain document to be violated, because I haven't provided the Prosecution with a copy of that document 20 hours in advance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may supplement a little bit on this issue. The Prosecution has the burden of proof, and we have documents that we've gathered through our own investigation. We don't know what the Prosecution is going to do, we don't know what the witness is going to say. We think, and I believe it would be a violation of the right to remain silent, in a sense, if we were to disclose our documents to the Prosecutor before they conduct their direct examination, because then they can then cure whatever problems we may have. It's a little bit like playing poker. If I show my hand to the Prosecutor and I'm the only one showing it, now, he has to show his. He's got to tell us what his documents are because he has that burden of proof. And let's say that the witness comes up and Mr. Scott today decides that he's not going to go into a particular area, which is his choice. Then I might have given a document to Mr. Scott that I might be able to use down the road with another witness, and now he begins to know what my strategy is, what my defence is, and he begins to do what I would call a rebuttal in his case in chief. I dare say that that would be improper. I think the best practice is, and I know that we disagree on this point, the Prosecution would like to have all the Defence documents at this time, even though we're still getting part of their documents. But I think it would be a violation of the right to remain silent. It's also -- we would be helping the Prosecution in meeting its burden. They don't need any help. If by now they can't figure out what their case is and they can't put on their case, then they certainly don't need any help from me. So I would ask Your Honours that we not -- that we not be put in a position where we have to disclose our documents to them until we decide. And I may not make that decision. Even, for instance, yesterday, I had plenty of documents that I was prepared to use. However, based on the cross-examination, I chose not to. That was a decision that was made at that instance. I'm going to save them for some other time. So, Your Honours, I would ask you to take that into consideration. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. Scott. Please answer these three points: First point, the issue of the laptop, laptops that will be given to the accused. They would use them during the hearing, after which the CD would be burned and taken by the accused, possibly to use it later on the computer -- computers they have in the Detention Unit in Scheveningen. That's the first issue. Second issue, and I need your advice before I speak to Mr. Registrar and the President of the Tribunal about this, the Defence counsel are of my view, which was a personal view, I think it would be more useful for the accused to be next to their lawyers. I'd like to know what you think of this. Third issue, but this is something that crops up in every trial proceedings, that's the issue of documents during cross-examination. The Defence tells us that you have the burden of proof, so they don't have to tell you in advance what they plan to use in terms of documents. Therefore, that you would only be apprised of the documents at the last minute inasmuch as the Prosecution have the burden of proof and the Defence do not have to make the Prosecution's life easier. So on these three issues very quickly, Mr. Scott, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, on the laptop issue, we have no position except that whatever security issues may be raised. There maybe some security issues or concerns about the transfer of information, that sort of thing. Other than that, we have no particular position. We defer to the security staff on the best practice. And the same position on the second part. As far as where the accused sit in the courtroom, as far as I'm concerned, that's entirely a matter of security. I think we should defer to the expertise of the security staff. And this has been the practice in the last ten years of this Tribunal, it's been the practice for the accused to sit together in the box, so to speak, arranged as they are today, with security arranged as they are today. The Tribunal's been doing that for the last 10 or 12 years, it seems like there's no reason to change that now. I think we should defer to the expertise of the security staff. On the issue of cross-examination documents, Your Honour, I'm glad this has come up. I think what has been said this morning is actually quite telling, and you're going to see this time and time again day in and day out in the next couple of years. The apparent philosophy is that while the Prosecution should turn over, of course, every single possible piece of paper in advance and provide a fair trial, the Defence should not provide a fair trial to the Prosecution, and for the Prosecution it is trial by ambush. That is, they can wait and spring everything they have on us at the last minute, including documents coming up on the screen at the moment that we've never seen before, having no idea where it came from, whether the witness has ever seen it before, what its origins are, anything; we see a document pop up on the screen for the first time. I think that is fundamentally unfair. In connection with the preparation for cross-examination, Your Honours, let's remember this: By the time a Prosecution witness comes into the courtroom, there has been extensive disclosure. All that witness's prior statements have been disclosed to the Defence. Numerous documents have been provided. We have provided already a list of the documents that will be used with the witness. They have this now, they have it now for the witnesses in July. They know, with a few exceptions, inevitably, there will be something that we missed that will be added, but for the most part these Defence teams now know the exhibits that we will use with witnesses who are coming in July. That's reflected in the chart that we provided to the Chamber. So they have the prior statements, they have the Rule 65 ter summary that tells what the witness is going to say, basically, and they have all the documentation. Now with all respect to Defence counsel, I respect their function, I respect the amount of work involved; at the same time, they have a very good idea when that witness comes into the courtroom what will basically be said. Yes, there are sometimes a bit of variation, a little bit -- a little darker shade of grey, a little bit of this, a little bit of that, but fundamentally the witness's testimony is basically known, anticipated. The cross-examination is prepared -- I'm sure, I'm confident that the Defence begin their cross-examination preparation well before the witness ever takes the stand. Now, in that situation, Your Honour, I think it is fundamentally unfair to the Prosecution to be receiving these exhibits one by one, literally as they pop up on the screen in front us. And we would ask to be -- we would ask to be provided the cross-examination exhibits one day before the cross-examination is expected to begin, and that is being done in other cases. In the Vukovar case that is going on right now, the Defence teams are required -- the Defence is required to provide their exhibits one day in advance. I do not think that is unreasonable. As I said several days ago, the Prosecution, Your Honour -- Your Honours, is also entitled to favour trial. It has nothing to do with the burden of proven. Of course we have the burden of proof and we will meet that burden of proof, but we're also entitled to a fair trial and it is not fair for documents to be sprung on us for the first time, there has been no disclosure, we don't see these documents, and all of a sudden a document shows up on the screen for the first time and we are expected to deal with it. I think that's fundamentally unfair, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Just one question to you, Mr. Karnavas. In the United States - I say that specifically, in the United States - during cross-examination do Defence teams present documents at the last minute or are they under the obligation under federal rules to submit the document to the Prosecution one day before? One day or two before.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excellent question. Excellent question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As all the questions by the Judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's at the moment I deliver it. I have absolutely no obligation, none, zero obligation to provide the Prosecution in advance. It's the moment that I stand up there and I present it. Now, because we're dealing with a jury, there's always the issue of a foundation, and sometimes if we're going to have some problems we may deal with that outside the presence of the jury but I have absolutely no obligation to present that. And if I might just add a retort to what Mr. Scott said, in other cases, unlike the one that he pointed, in the Halilovic case, for instance, it was just popping up at the moment that they were introducing the document. And I dare say it is fundamentally unfair for me to be showing my hand in advance because he's going to do something with that document. That's the problem. I share, you know, his concerns, and my heart goes out to him, but, you know, he's got a lot of help. He's got a lot of help. Now, if I could just give you an example, Your Honour. We left yesterday the courtroom. We went back and it was until midnight that I was working to figure out which documents I'm going to be using. Here's the problem: Yes, they provided us this list. They provided it late. I don't want to go into that issue, but needless to say, we got it rather late. I don't have the sort of team that can prepare weeks in advance. My nose is just above the water. We're getting ready for two very important witnesses. One gave six testimonies. Imagine now how -- what my weekend is going to be like. I'm not crying sour grapes, but they can cry me a river when it comes to, you know, the difficulties they have. They have no idea. Let them come on this side of the bench and figure out how it is. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very quickly, because we could spend hours on this. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If you are interested, and then you just tell me whether you are or I will not talk further. Since you ask what is the situation in US law, perhaps it would be interesting to hear what is, let's say, the criminal proceeding law in Croatia, one of the involved countries. And I guess, as much as I know, it is more or less the same in Bosnia-Herzegovina, because most laws originated from the former, which was quite the same one. If you want me to explain, I will. If you don't, I will not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please go ahead quickly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, in our criminal proceedings there is no obligation for the Defence to produce any evidence, any document to the Prosecution before the moment the Defence choose to do so. So whenever I as a lawyer, as a Defence counsel, choose to present the document either to the witness, Prosecution witness or Defence witness, which we may not call that in this these proceedings because there the witnesses are always witnesses of the Court, but, however, one of them is positive to you, one is not. So I can take a document from my bag and put it on the table in the very moment of the testimony. No restrictions on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Ms. Nozica.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I would just briefly like to support what my colleagues before me have already said, and to add that the Prosecutor told us today about his obligations as provided for by the Rules, and this Prosecutor is duty-bound to disclose material to us. But I'd like to indicate something that happened yesterday which can objectively be a great problem. If we were to disclose our documents 24 hours ahead, we could jeopardise our own Defence. And yesterday, we had prepared a certain number of exhibits. Had we provided them to the Prosecutor earlier on, we would have disclosed our main lines of Defence, our Defence case to the Prosecutor. So yesterday we did not disclose this because the direct or, rather, the examination-in-chief went in a completely different direction. It did not follow the direction we expected it to take. And today we're going to examine the witness in chief, we're going to continue the cross-examination, so to disclose our exhibits in advance to the Prosecutor could seriously jeopardise the rights of our clients. And for this reason, and I'd like to associate myself with the demands made by my colleagues, that we be allowed to disclose our evidence when we present it. And if there are any problems in establishing the origin of the documents, as you yourself said, this can be done subsequently through various submissions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall discuss this among Judges, and we will tell you what to do. In the meantime, let's have the witness in, because we are already half an hour late. Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I can use the time efficiently. One or two items as the witness comes in the courtroom. Just a final comment. I don't know how many times in the last 12 years I've been told that US practice does not govern this Tribunal. I always thought this Tribunal was trying to do better than US practice. I say that as a US lawyer myself. So I don't think this Tribunal is governed by, controlled by US practice at all. Secondly, Your Honour, this witness will also -- I want to supplement the earlier references. This witness will also give evidence relevant to count 2 and count 3 and count 26, which were not originally listed in the preparation papers, and his evidence is also relevant to paragraph 113 of the amended indictment. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Scott. Did you want to add something?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: No. That's it, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Good morning, sir. Before your solemn declaration I would like to have your surname, first name, date of birth, your occupation in 1992, 1993, and possibly your present occupation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you for those warm words. My name is Ratko Pejanovic. I am from Mostar. During 1991 to 1995, I was both the commander of the firefighting unit and a firefighter myself in Mostar. Today I'm retired, and I'm here before you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. What is your birth date?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was born on the 14th of January, 1944, in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question before you read the solemn declaration. Have you ever been a witness before a national or international court on the events that took place in your town in 1992 or until 1994, or is this the first time you're being a witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the first time that I find myself in the role of witness before an international court of law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Please read the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Thank you, sir. Please sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before the Prosecutor puts his questions to you, let me inform you on this: As you know, your testimony is scheduled today and tomorrow. You will first answer questions by the Prosecution. Once the Prosecution has finished, the Defence counsel will put questions to you. This is what we call in legal language cross-examination. There may be a re-direct examination by the Prosecution, and the four Judges before you could at any time, if they deem it necessary, ask questions of you. You've just made your solemn declaration. You're supposed to tell the truth. You are not supposed to tell lies, because this is a crime that can be punished by this Tribunal. If you feel tired, if you're not feeling well, say so straight away so that we can have a break, because it's quite tiring to testify for hours on end. And if you were to feel the slightest problem, do not hesitate to tell me so. Everybody here has breaks from time to time, every 90 minutes. So we'll have a 15-minute break first, and then you will have a lunch break, 50 minutes - it's not the usual time - and then we will resume in the afternoon. If at any moment you want to ask me something, do not hesitate. We are here to make your testimony easily -- as easy as possible. So if you need to put a question, just put it. Without further ado, I give the floor to Mr. Scott, who is going to put his questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Pejanovic.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just to briefly touch on an item or two that Mr. President has already touched upon, you were born in Mostar in January, 1944, and have lived there all your life; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And by ethnicity or nationality you are a Serb; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you have spent most of your working life working as a -- or did spend it as a fireman or a firefighter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When did you first start working as a professional firefighter in Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: If I may be allowed to digress for a moment. In July, 1991 -- no, I apologise. In 1981 I began working as the commander of the volunteer firefighting unit and an instructor of the firefighting association which, at the time, had 38 units.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In the interests of time, sir, I want to jump quickly to the time period 1991, 1992. Can you describe for the Judges what the firefighting organisation was in the city of Mostar up -- in the time 1991 up until approximately the middle of 1992. How many firefighting units were there in the city? How was it organised?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Since before the war, a long time before the war, the fire brigade association of Mostar had 13 firefighting units. In 1991, sometime in September, with the arrival of the reservists in Mostar, certain things had to be changed radically, because many of the voluntary units in town, especially in the work collectives, ceased functioning, and it was just the professional units that continued working, the professional firefighting company and the Mostar volunteers. We continued working until April, sometime around April, 1992, and in that period of time, in view of the bad relations in town, because incidents began in the cafes in town, hand grenades were thrown in front of the courtyard of the Orthodox church, for example; there would be machine-gun fire during the night. I don't know where, but I know I could hear it, because I live nearby, and this was terrible because it was at a distance of 300 metres as the crow flies. Anyway, the fire brigade, the firefighters at that time had the task of doing duty work in shifts, especially in our volunteer association. There would be two firefighters on duty and one driver per shift, and one of those three individuals was the duty officer by the telephone. This was duty work in the unit itself. We tried to maintain the equipment and everything because very often people stormed shops and things like that. Incidents broke out. So that is why we organised ourselves in this way, and that went up to the 18th or, to be exact, 19th of April, 1992, when a meeting was held with the -- all the commanders of the units and staffs of the Civil Defence, civilian protection, and I was invited to attend because at that time, in addition to my professional duties as commander of the firefighting unit, I was also the commander of the civilian protection unit. And already at that time the need was seen for the service to be organised in a different manner for the simple reason that within the composition of the civilian protection there were two detachments that were associated, and there were two firefighting units within that detachment. The general call to mobilisation was put out but none of the members responded, and we -- I saw how we could organise the service in order to maintain a minimum of manpower in the unit and allow the unit to work when needed in town. And my proposal was this: That we take over part of the people that, according to their military schedule written down in their military booklet, should become part of the firefighters of Mostar. There were very few people who belonged to other structures. So in this way, I was able to set up a team of some 30 men by pooling our resources, and at my personal request I received a written order from the civilian defence staff which was signed at that time by the president or, rather, the commander of the Civil Defence staff, Mr. Roko Markovina [phoen]. Finally, at the end of that order, along with some other documents I published in a book that I wrote in 1997 and published.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Very well. Let me clarify a couple of points in your answer before we proceed further. You made reference, that in approximately the first part or mid-1992 there was increasing conflict and tension in Mostar. Now, was this conflict between at that time Serbs and non-Serbs primarily?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Unfortunately, that is how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you feel -- did you -- were you the recipient or did you feel any of this tension or pressure being a Serb yourself, sir, in Mostar at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to be quite frank, I myself did not have any serious problems, although there were some provocations. They said why don't I bring out my weapons? Where are my weapons? Did I have any weapons? And one night when I was on duty with my other neighbours in the street I lived in, because each street had established this duty work, and when I think about that, I don't know why I did this duty work, because I had no weapons, but anyway, I was present there and did these shifts together with my neighbours. As I had already been on duty for 24 hours in the firefighting unit, I took with me a little walkie-talkie because I thought that if there was an interruption in telephone communications I could have communication with my men, and if need be they could call me up. And on one occasion we had a code. I was 101, for example, number 101, and they would call me up not to use names, not to have to use names. And one night some of the neighbours around me, they were mostly Serbs, said, "Why have you got this walkie-talkie? What are you doing in the station there?" And that was the last time I did duty with my neighbours. I was with my firefighters for 24 hours after that and I would just go home to have a change of clothing and refresh myself and things like that while you were able to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness kindly be asked to slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If you received that translation, sir, if you could possibly slow down just a little bit. The interpreters and those in the courtroom would appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't hear that, but, yes, thank you for cautioning me. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please. Again, sir, to clarify, you said a few moments ago, you said, "They said, Why don't you bring out your weapons? Where are my weapons?" You made several references to "they." Who is the "they" you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I said they were my neighbours. For the most part Serbs, because in that street where we lived, there was an ethnic mix of inhabitants. There were Bosniaks and Serbs and Croats. A little fewer Croats, perhaps, but at that point in time we were all there together and we were all doing duty work together. And generally that provocation - and I consider it to be a provocation to this day - it came from the mouths of -- well, my compatriots, if I can put it that way; the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And you mentioned reference -- you made a reference to an organisation called civilian protection. Can you tell us a bit more about that, just very briefly, please, about what that organisation was. Was that part of the municipal government or what was -- what was civilian protection?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Civilian protection was a component part of the municipal government. It existed from previous times. It was not a novelty that was introduced. It existed as part of the reorganisation of the country, and it had as its aim to rally around it units and formations which were able, with their materiel, technical equipment, and manpower, to intervene in moments of crisis such as large-scale disasters, earthquakes, floods possibly, large-scale fires, and so on. The structure was mixed. There were units to deal with the situation, decontamination units, and in this joint detachment there was a local service, two detachments with one firefighting unit in each. As such, we were called upon at times when the need arose for any defence to be organised, defence or protection when an aggression was launched.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention, please, to approximately the 31st of July, 1992. Did your position change at that time? You had been commander of the firefighting unit. Did your position change around July of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Unfortunately, yes. And it's very painful for me to stress this, only for the fact that I was a Serb. On the 15th of July, 1992, a man turned up. I know his surname was Jugo, I don't know his first name. But quite simply he came and said to me that I was no longer the unit commander as of that day and that to replace me would be Meho Kekic. He would take my place. He was a young man who was trained in the firefighting unit of which I was a commander and trainer/instructor. He was a young man. But that's what happened. And I also have to stress that at that point in time, another man was supposed to replace me, a commander who was a Croat, and his name was Miroslav Mrdjo. But within the staff, two Bosniaks were opposed to that appointment, and they demanded that it be a representative of the Bosniak ethnic group who would be the commander of the unit, because in other structures changes had already been made. So that is how I was replaced as commander of the unit by Mr. Meho Kekic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you have any understanding as to why you were dismissed or replaced as commander at that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: To be quite frank, yes, I did. I knew very clearly why that happened. And since I was replaced only by word of mouth, without any written evidence, and I had taken up my duties as commander and was appointed as commander quite clearly on the basis of a written order, I asked to be received by the president of the civilian protection at that time, who was Mr. Josip Skutor. And I have to say quite frankly that I needed a lot of time to set up the appointment and to talk to the man. When I did get to talk to him, I asked him that he issue me a paper on my dismissal and replacement, just as I had received my appointment papers when I came to lead the unit. And I also asked for a statement of reasons why I was being replaced, but I never received an answer. I was never told the reasons for my replacement, although it was clear to me why, and I published what I did get from them in writing later on in my book.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said it was clear to you why. What was -- what was the reason?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: The reason was exclusively my ethnic affiliation, because at that time, generally speaking, in town everyone who was not [as interpreted] a Croat or a Serb was replaced, or all things Croatian and Serbian were replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Judges where you -- you continued to work, though. You weren't the commander, but you continued to work as the -- in the fire department or in the firefighting unit; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. But it's also correct, and I have to say again quite bitterly, that I remained in my duty as a firefighter, and I felt like a clay pigeon. It was only a matter of time who would pull the trigger first. And you -- it's a terrible realisation when you were the creator of a unit that saw the light of day exclusively thanks to your efforts, that you are just somebody who wasn't allowed to drive the car, to take up a walkie-talkie, to report when a fire had broken out or to communicate with their colleagues in the field if they needed assistance and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: In line 18 it should say everyone who was a Croat or a Serb was replaced, without the "not." Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: In July, 1992, sir, as part of the Mostar government, can you tell the Judges what political party or organisation controlled the Mostar government as of the summer of 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to mention that on the 30th of June, 1992, there was a military coup effected by the HVO, and the legally elected government was completely replaced. That is to say everything that happened and that was won at the elections, beginning with the lord mayor, and later everybody else, was replaced and military officials replaced them and took the key positions in town. And the president of the HVO, at least that is what it says in the signature, was Jadranko Topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you say that everything that happened, everyone that had won the elections beginning with the lord mayor and later everybody who was replaced, who replaced these previously elected officials? From what group or organisation or what political parties would these new people, these new officials come?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we have to accept one particular fact, and that is that a point in time three national parties won the election and took over power in town; the HDZ, SDS, and SDA. When the Serbs left town, not to say that the SDS left town, all that remained was -- there was no SDS. So what remained was the SDA and HDZ. And the HDZ had the main say. As I say, it was them who conducted the military coup when they replaced the legally elected people, the leading figures, beginning with the lord mayor onwards. And then the town administration, municipal administration, was left without one ethnic group. It just disappeared. And the Serbs that remained remained as a bargaining chip, and that -- a population of that nature. I remained within the unit at that point, but I told you what great -- high price I had to pay for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This Mr. Skutor who came to you and dismissed you as commander, what ethnic group was he from?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: He's a Croat. He was a representative of the civilian protection in the government in Mostar at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, going forward, you remained in the fire department. Did you -- can you tell the Judges where the firefighting building or location was where you worked at that time.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the 11th of May, 1992, the fire department was in Braca Brkica Street number 4, opposite the department store called Razvitak. On the 11th of May, 1992, my assessment was that the Serbs were exerting a lot of pressure on the left bank and that more and more people were leaving the left bank, and the fire brigade also participated in the evacuation of people on a number of occasions. We helped those who wanted to leave the left bank leave. We evacuated them. On the 11th of May, I went to my flat. I came across a Serbian unit in my street, and afterwards, I believe that I would never have stayed on in such -- in such conditions. Part of the unit had already been moved to the right bank. I told them about the situation, and at that point in time there was someone called Miodrag Kandic, a Serb, there. There were two brothers Dostovic, Edo and Nerko. They were Bosniaks. Four of us remained there, and the others were on the right bank of the river. I said I didn't know whether we could carry on living there, but we could have surrendered to the Serbs, surrendered all our equipment to the Serbs, we could have gone over to the Serbs, but I just cross the Neretva because this idea didn't even occur to me, because that area was attacked by snipers, and that will be the case for days. We moved over to the right bank, and then we found accommodation with colleagues of ours in a firefighting company, and we then asked to move to another location. We moved to the institute of the construction university. We were there for a while and operated from that area. We went to put fires out from that area. We knew exactly which area we should cover in case fire broke out, and we remained in that location up until the month of September. We then returned to our previous premises. But on the 18th of June, 1992, we were in the pupils' home as well as the location at the left bank. We had these two locations, and at this other location we had the group of five men, and every day we'd cross over and provide people with food and logistics support. Every two or three days the shift would change. If there was a lot of pressure on the right bank, we would stay on for seven days. So from the 18th of June, there were two locations that we had; on the left bank in our old premises, and on the right bank in the pupil's home. That was up until September. And after September we returned to our initial premises.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. A couple of points before we move to 1993, sir. When you talk -- it may be early enough in the trial, but just to be clear, when you talk about -- when you say the right bank, you're preferring -- you're referring primarily to west -- what might be called West Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. I don't know how to put it, but our base was in Brace Brkica Street number 4, opposite the Razvitak department store. That was our base. But if we had to look for a new location, a new base, then I can't really say that we moved to the eastern part of town or the northern part of town. We went to the right bank for a certain purpose; to preserve the people and the equipment, and to an extent we were successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, my question was actually more basic than that, just by clarification of terminology. When you refer to the left bank and the right bank, I just want the record to be clear and to assist the Judges. When you say the right bank, is that a reference to what might also be called West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's certain.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And when you say the left bank, that is a reference to what also might be called East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: The eastern part of Mostar, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have this map, 9517. It might be easier to submit this to the witness for more clarity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We are going to get into that map rather extensively, Your Honour. I had not planned on getting to it just yet. If I might -- with the Court's permission, if I might delay getting into that for a few more months. I think his testimony - I hope - is now clear on that point.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, you -- you told us so far this morning that by the summer of 1992, the HDZ -- what was then the HDZ, the Croat political party, had taken control of the town and that most other people -- the previously elected officials were -- had been -- had been dismissed or replaced. I just want to refer back to your testimony. And for counsel and the Court, this is at page 24, line 17. You talked about everyone in town "who was not a Croat or a Serb" being replaced. Was it all the Croats and Serbs being replaced or was it non-Croats being replaced?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try and repeat what I said a minute ago. I said that the legal authorities of the town of Mostar were completely replaced. Even the mayor, who was a Croat, he was also replaced. He was replaced too. The fact that he was a Croat was of not much assistance to him. He was replaced because he probably didn't toe the HDZ line. And all the others who shared the mayor's ideas, Mr. Gagro Milivoj, for example, were replaced. That was also the case with the Bosniaks who didn't accept the policies pursued by the HDZ at that time. So regardless of the ethnic group they belonged to, if you weren't part of their team, if you didn't follow their ideas, you would be replaced. And I apologise. I said that since the Serbs left the town, they were no longer there. There were military authorities in the town who stayed on, and all the others who stayed on, well, they had to make do as best they could.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, before we go on to 1993, let me direct your attention to an event in 1992. Did anyone attempt to take your vehicle away from you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, only on one occasion. I found out about certain things from my daughter, and I bought two and two together, because at one point in time she started crying. She said, "Dad, please take care of yourself. Don't forget that I'm the only person you have," and that really affected me. So I didn't really know what my daughter knew at the time. I said I'm now doing something for the benefit of the town, and naturally she said, "What good will that do if I find myself in a difficult situation?" And then she said, "Dad, are you aware of the fact they're following you in town?" I had no idea that that was the case. She then mentioned the detail. When I put everything together, I realised that the child was right. She was with her aunt in Siroki Brijeg at the time and she would have obtained information from the young people that she socialised with. Earlier on I was escorting a member of ours because at one point in time he asked for me to provide him with 10 firefighters in the aluminium institute. I took him to part of the Rudnik -- to part of Rudnik, which is about three kilometres away from our location. It's in the western part of town. And when we were in the vicinity of Rudnik, where he was to report to, there was a nest or there was a location with obstacles. There were two uniformed men wearing the insignia Territorial Defence, they stopped me, and they said -- or one of them said that I should get out of the car. It wasn't my car, I said. How was I to leave the car? They said, Just get out and let's have your driving licence and then you can go. And then a man of average height approached the person who had ordered me to do this, and he said, You know that we've agreed that you should leave firefighting vehicles and ambulance alone. Return the documents to this man. I had already given this member my driving licence. He returned the document, and this man then said, Sit down and drive off. I then took the young man away about 800 metres further. I said that he only had another 200 metres to go, and at that point I turned around. I didn't go to that part of town again until we moved to the other part of town and set -- found a premises in the pupils' home. We then had to fight fires when fires broke out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you know the name or come to know the name of this person who confronted you and wanted your papers and equipment?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. But I could point out that before that event occurred, since the firefighters would often provide people with water during peacetime if there was no water supply in certain areas, there was a reservoir of water that had been ordered, and usually you would take the address of the person who had requested water. So the person who had ordered water then said he was located in an area where there was no water supply, in the direction of Krusevo. He said that he would wait at Banovac. He would wait for the reservoir, for water to arrive there. It's in the direction of the western part of town. Naturally the driver received an order from the commander, he drove the truck of water to Banovac. When he arrived there, two men were waiting for him with rifles. They took him out of the vehicle and took the vehicle away and the vehicle ended up in Siroki Brijeg. And even a few years ago, the problem still hadn't been solved. I don't know if the vehicle has been returned now. This was a situation of anarchy, and all means were used to appropriate equipment from a certain environment. It didn't matter to whom the equipment belonged to, all they wanted to do was to steal equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again for the purposes of the record, I need to clarify when you say "they." You just said "all they wanted to do was to steal equipment." Who is the "they" you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, a while ago I said that they had the chequerboard emblem on their left sleeves, and it said Territorial Defence beneath that chequerboard. I later assumed that they were HVO forces, since they had Territorial Defence insignia on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which of the armed forces in your experience in the area of Mostar at that time wore chequerboard insignia?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, look, on the whole the HVO, and any men who were part of the HVO, regardless of the nationality of those men, they would have such an insignia. I have my civilian protection booklet. The old ones were taken away, but they issued new ones with an introduction in the Croatian language and with the chequerboard emblem. You have the Croatian flag and then you have the chequerboard on these booklets. So that means that civilian protection members who were part of those formations had these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you -- can you assist --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: We had these emblems in our booklets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you assist the Chamber, please: When were these new documents and papers with the Croatian flag and the Croatian insignia, when were these papers issued to you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was around June, the end of June, or in July. I couldn't tell you when exactly. I really don't remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Which year?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- but I think it was towards the end of July. In 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I want to direct your attention now to early 1993, and can you tell the Chamber if anything happened in terms of the reorganisation of the firefighting units in Mostar at that time in January of 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes. You could put it that way. You could say that they were reorganised, because on the 22nd of January, 1993, a decision was taken according to which the fire brigade should be reorganised. It was very important for the operations of the Mostar firefighting units. We were informed of this decision around the 28th, but the decision was taken on the 23rd of January, I believe. The decision states that the Mostar firefighting organisation shall make available all its equipment to the professional firefighting company. The Niva vehicle should be provided to the civilian protection staff, to the head of the staff, Mr. Josip Skutor. The firefighting unit would be dismantled and would be mobilised when necessary. How to mobilise a unit to intervene, if you've taken its equipment, how can it intervene in such a case? What sort of function can such a unit have?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the official who issued this decision?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Of course. Jadran Topic. That's the signature you can see. And I've published this document, or the document appears in the book that I published.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could have the assistance of the Registry, please, to display Exhibit P09511. 9511.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us what that document is, sir. If you've seen it before and what it is.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I've had this document in my hands and it appears in my book. And this confirms everything that I said. The Mostar fire brigade is being ordered to provide the fire brigade company with its equipment. They have to provide Mr. Josip Skutor with equipment, and the unit is being dismantled. I have to point out that we never carried out this order. We didn't want to carry it out.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Why not?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: We didn't want to carry it out for the simple reason that all of a sudden 30 men would have been left without any work. Anyone could have captured them and organised them in a way that they saw fit. But this was equipment that belonged to the volunteer fire brigade. So I won't be modest now, but I must say that in -- as far as 80 per cent of the equipment that they were requesting is concerned, I personally, together with my colleagues, gave up part of our salaries to obtain that equipment. We paid for that equipment, that firefighting equipment, ourselves, and as a result, I was against this decision, and we were unanimous in rejecting this decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, sir, around this same time in January of 1993, did -- were there any changes made in the way that your daily food ration was provided to you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They issued this order. We refused to comply with it. On the following day, when our people went to the northern camp, which is where we received logistics support and food from, they were simply told that they could no longer obtain food there. So we then went to army members, armija members, informed them of the fact, and they provided us with food and logistics support just as they provided such things to their own men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Once again, Mr. Pejanovic, I need your assistance, please. When you say "they issued this order," who again was the "they"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's now quite clear that "they" refers to the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. It says Jadranko Topic at the bottom of the document. It's quite clear he was the president of the HVO. They also refer to decisions taken in 1992, and to an extent in 1991. And that was prior to all these events in that area. Prior to all these events, there were preparations for the organisation of Herceg-Bosna. And this can be quite clearly seen in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Forgive me, sir. My question perhaps was not clear enough. When I referred to just now about the -- I was talking about the situation with the food, and when the situation changed and someone -- someone, "they," changed the situation in reference to your daily food ration, who was "they" or what organisation was "they"?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat what I said. It's quite clear that they are HVO members. It's quite clear that this formation had already organised itself in Herceg-Bosna. As to who is behind this, as to who is behind the person who signed the document, Jadranko Topic, I don't know. It would be difficult for me to provide anyone else's name, but you can see that Jadranko Topic is concerned. If you have a look at this document, he was probably someone who had been authorised to act in Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Did you -- were you ever given any reason why the HVO stopped providing you food, the firefighters in your unit food in January 1993?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. President, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would kindly ask that the question be rephrased. He's referring to Herceg-Bosna. He's not saying who it was. He refers to Mr. Topic. The question now about -- posed by Mr. Scott is that the HVO. So I would ask that the question be rephrased. It assumes a fact that's definitely not in evidence, at least at this point in time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll be happy to rephrase it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Mr. Scott. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The -- did you receive any explanation or reason from the Herceg-Bosna organisation at that time as to why you were no longer be providing -- provided food?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. We didn't receive any explanations. This is not something we could check, but it was quite clear to us. We refused to execute their order or their decision, so naturally we were punished by not being provided with logistic support. That's quite logical. But once again, it was impossible for us to verify why this had taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a couple more questions on this topic, if we could continue. Then we would finish that before the break, or I'm in the Chamber's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I would like, with the Registry's assistance, for you to please now be shown Exhibit P09512. Can you tell us, please, what that document is.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that the document speaks for itself. You can quite clearly see that this is the Croatian Defence Council as a component part of the Republic of Herceg-Bosna, the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, which orders that the voluntary firefighting association should be deleted. And when we received this decision that we were no longer part of the civilian protection of Mostar, I have to note that as of the 23rd of January, when we refused to carry out the decision by which they had decided to do this, we were no longer within the composition of that formation. And this was officially written on the 3rd of May. Please remember this date, the 3rd of May. Make a note of it, because subsequent events will be very important when you look at this date, the 3rd of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, this Mr. Skutor, who is on the document Exhibit 9512, is this the same Mr. Skutor who had previously removed you from your command position?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it's the same person.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, that completes my questions on this topic, if the Court would like to take a break at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As I told you, we will have a 15-minute break. We shall resume around quarter to eleven.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We can now continue with the hearing. You may take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, right before the break you -- you exhorted us to the be very mindful of the date of the 3rd of May, 1993, and I indeed now want to take you to May, 1993, and particularly direct your attention to the 9th of May. Can you tell us, please, what happened on that day, and if there's something that you want to tell the Chamber that happened sometime also in early May, the 3rd of May, or between the 3rd of May and the 9th of May, please do so.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: A little earlier on, I said that I wanted to focus on this date as it's very important date. It was the 3rd of May. And on the 9th of May, a conflict broke out between the HVO and the ABiH, or between the Croats and the Muslims. That's when the conflict broke out. There was a decision on the 23rd of January, according to which the Mostar fire brigade was to hand over its equipment to the firefighting company, and it was supposed to hand over the vehicle, its vehicle, to the civilian protection. With this decision, I think their objective was quite specifically stated. Now, I'm asking you, what would have happened if we had carried out that order dated the 23rd of January? And if we take into consideration the 3rd of May decision, on 9th of May, all the citizens of Mostar would have had to go down to the river to collect water in the event of difficulties. So, luckily, we didn't comply with the order. Let me just paraphrase this. But we managed to provide an elementary form of protection to the town by using our equipment. We could provide them with a certain amount of water. And that's why I said that the 3rd of May was an extremely important date.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, let me direct you further to specifically the 9th of May. Can you tell us what you recall about that day. What happened to you and to the firefighting unit in East Mostar on that day? Or West Mostar, but wherever you were.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: At that time, we were already in Brkica Street, opposite the Razvitak department store. The unit was formed of the night-shift. I was in the night shift from Saturday to Sunday. On Sunday I was supposed to hand over my duties to someone else. At about quarter to five in the morning, shooting broke out. We were lying down. We couldn't really determine where the shooting was coming from or who was shooting. It took us a while to wake up and to come to our senses. We then realised that the shooting was coming from the direction of the Bulevar. That is in fact where the demarcation line was established later on. I agreed on a -- taking certain action with my colleague. We thought that -- in fact, we thought that the consequences wouldn't be very serious. So I went to the firefighting vehicle to take some water, because we had decided to make some coffee. And then I noticed that in front of our premises, 20 metres further down the road, there was a private house, and I could see some smoke coming out of the house. I told the men, let's forget the coffee and let's put the fire out. So we set off to put the fire out. But while we were putting the fire out, a sniper opened fire on us and he hit and penetrated two tubes, two pipes. When we saw that the shooting was quite frequent, we tried to move the firefighting vehicle, because opposite the road from where we were working there was an old facility, and in the basement of that building there were radio amateurs. And we tried to move the vehicle behind that building to protect it. We managed to continue using the hose to put the fire out. We also used certain items that we had found to partially protect the pipes. That was the first fire we tried to put out that day. In the course of that day there was an entire series of fires. And one of the fires I would like to underline was the fire at the police station, which was down by the market in the premises of the ship association, a sort of marine association. Naturally they had logistics support and weapons, food, and ammunition in the basement. They slept in another part of the building. We managed to put the fire out. It didn't spread to other surrounding buildings. That was a fairly difficult fire to deal with, but I think that in the course of that day we had between seven or eight interventions. We had seven or eight fires to put out, and as far as that specific fire is concerned, we put it out without suffering any consequences, and neither the men nor the equipment were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell the Chamber, please, whether the fire station, the headquarters of the firefighting unit, was struck by artillery fire on at that day, the 9th of May.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Our facility and the location where it was located was frequently targeted. Let me just tell you this: The top portion of the fire tower was hit twice severely. One of the shells broke through the tower and landed on the facility, and the other shell knocked out the crown of the tower, which was -- which topped the tower. There was also a construction beam which went through the whole building. It was the main beam, and all other beams were touching it or lying across it, so this beam had to be replaced. We watched the consequences of that particular shelling, and we realised that this is what was damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: You said a moment ago that throughout the day of the 9th of May you and your unit responded to approximately seven to eight separate fires. Apart from the fire station, can you tell the Judges any other locations that you remember that were struck by artillery fire on that day.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I told you a minute ago that the police station had been set on fire. It was targeted from a hill called Hum hill. This is where they had very good visibility from. Also on that same day there was an institute of hygiene that was targeted. It used to be the institute of hygiene and then became a war hospital, and it was protected by sandbags, and beams, once again, were damaged by missiles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can you tell us -- Mr. Pejanovic, we're going to come back in a few minutes to some of the specific incidents of shellings and fires that you were involved -- that you were involved in, but before we do that, after -- once the events of the 9th of May had taken place, can you tell the Judges, please, a bit more about what was done to mobilise the firefighting forces in East Mostar once the conflict began in full earnest.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier in my evidence, I said that on the 9th of May I was supposed to leave my shift, which means that my entire shift was to leave, a new shift was to take up duty. All of our people had their houses in Western Mostar, their family homes, but there were also some of them who had their temporary residence in that part of town, in Western Mostar. After the conflict erupted, it wasn't reasonable to expect that people would arrive that morning to take up the shift, to take up duty. Therefore, I and other colleagues were forced to take in new people who had no experience or little experience. We simply had no choice. Therefore, at that point in time, we took in a lot of new personnel to work as firefighters. We even took in some people who used to be firefighters, were members of the fire brigade, and then left the brigade. For example, Sator Ahmet, Mirzo Bratic, who was later killed by shrapnel. I can give you some other names, but I don't know whether you're interested. These were mostly people who used to work at the fire brigade, worked there before the war and then, due to various circumstances, left the brigade, and then once the conflict erupted, they came back and rejoined brigade. Mirza Bratic, whom I mentioned, his parents used to live in a building called Beirut, which is near the bus and train station. As soon as conflict erupted, since he couldn't go to the other side, just like our people couldn't go to the other side, he came and reported to us, and I immediately accepted him into the unit. I have to mention that on that same day a fire broke out near the demarcation line, near Santica Street and the cinema building. Since the order had been issued excluding us from the staff and this area belonged to sector 1, we called up our colleagues and told them that several apartments were on fire. They went to the location, and I don't know what happened, but they were caught in the crossfire between the HVO and the BH army. And then there were also members of the BH MUP there. They left the engine out in the street, and then they fled and took shelter. They didn't know what was happening, and we didn't know what was happening. Nobody told us anything, and their radio equipment remained in the engine. And then two or three days later, they called us up and accused us. They said we were to blame for the disappearance of two or three men who were there in that fire engine. So a colleague of mine and I took a car, we crossed the bridge, went to a location near Santica Street, and we went from one apartment to the next, calling out the names. And a woman came out of one of the apartments and she said, "They are here." So we found these men and we told them what happened, that we were being blamed for their disappearance. We told them that they need to call their families and tell them that they were fine. So that's what happened. And naturally everybody was pleased that they were found. We offered them to come and join us. They said that they would think about that. Since there was no food, no cigarettes, they were basically cut off from everything, on the following day they came to us, and they stayed for some 15 to 20 days, I'm not sure exactly of the time period. And they were wonderful young men. They helped a lot in various repairs, because, you know, daily we had to repair our engines, our vehicles, because we were using them under abnormal circumstances. And then in the meantime, Pompiers sans Frontieres came and joined us, our colleagues from France. They brought in some humanitarian aid, they brought a small water tank truck, and then an ambulance vehicle and some other items. They also brought IV fluids, about 1.000 litres of it. The ambulance vehicle, which was fully equipped, and the IV fluids were immediately turned over to the war hospital. We did it because they needed it. And they were getting ready to cross over into Western Mostar. It was organised by UNPROFOR. So we managed to include these four men into that convoy, and we sent them to the other side. Unfortunately - and I mean this sincerely - unfortunately, one of these colleagues, a fireman, after I started inquiring about them, and I started doing that early, inquiring and crossing over to the other side, so after I started doing that, I learned that one of them was killed by a sniper somewhere near the Bulevar. They went out on an intervention, and he was killed by a sniper. 11

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This time when some assistance arrived from the French organisation, the ambulance and some other assistance, can you give the Judges, please, an approximate date when this occurred; at least the month and the year?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I can tell you that it was sometime in late May when we sent them back. The event itself, when they came to put out fire, that was on the 9th of May in the afternoon, after 2.00 p.m. And I told you that they stayed with us for a while, and then in the meantime Pompiers sans Frontieres arrived, and somewhere in late May the convoy went to cross into the other part of the town and we had to negotiate with civilian authorities because everybody needed permits to cross over into the other part. So we somehow managed to do it with the military authorities and to ensure that they could go back.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: From what -- from what authority did you need a permit to enter into West Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: There was no chance for us to cross over into the other part of town. No. It was the convoy that went there, and it was arranged between two authorities. The convoy was led by UNPROFOR. And we tried to include our colleagues, firemen, in that convoy so they could leave Mostar, and together with them we sent our four colleagues, firemen, from the fire unit from the other bank. We included them in the convoy. We needed authorisation, both from civilian and military authorities from that part of the town in order to do that, because they checked the identity of persons in the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Around this time, sir, after May of 1993, did you once again become the commander of the firefighting unit in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It so happened that the colleague who was appointed in July of 1993 when I was removed from my position started creating trouble, first minor trouble and then more significant trouble for the civilian authorities. Almost daily there would be at least one complaint about his work, especially when it came to the distribution of water throughout town. Then civilian authorities got fed up with the complaints against him, and at one point in time they started wondering, is he the only one who can do this job, or are there any other people who can do that as well? And then some people who knew me from before the war, they said that, yes, that I was there, that my name was Ratko Pejanovic, but that I was a Serb. Literally, that's what they said. And then the president of the War Presidency, Mr. Smajo Kljajic, said, Well, what can I do? It's not my fault that he's a Serb. If he knows how to do this job, then let's appoint him to that position. And this is how on the 15th of July I was reappointed commander of the fire station. This is when the civilian authorities were in the process of being established on the left bank.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, I've been asked again to remind you if you could please speak a bit slower. The interpreters are trying to keep up with you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I truly apologise. Please don't take it against me. Even now as I speak about these events, I am re-experiencing them. I will do my best to try and control the speed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before we continue on, sir, you made a reference a moment ago, on page 46, line - we're about to lose it, in fact - line 8, the person, the colleague who was appointed, you said July of 1993. Were you referring, sir, to when you were replaced in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's possible that it was a slip of tongue. I apologise. My colleague, Meho Kekic, was appointed on -- in July of 1992, and I was removed. And then a year later, again in July, he was removed and I was re-appointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And as of this time, or as of May, 1993, sir, is it correct that with the exception of you, a Serb, that all the other members of the fire brigade in East Mostar were Muslim or Bosniak?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
