utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. It couldn't have been any other way, because there were no young personnel of Serb ethnicity, and none of them were really interested in that job. There were about 600 Serbs on the left bank, and those were mostly the elderly, and those who were younger joined either the BH MUP or the BH army, so they already belonged to a formation and couldn't join the fire brigade. As for the Croat residents, they were mostly the elderly. I think that there were 246 of them. I just happen to have these figures because sometime in June, May or June of 1994, we distributed some food that was given to the Serbian civic council, whose president I was. So this food was given to us and then we distributed it, and I knew, because of that, how many residents there were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Let me next turn your attention, please, to -- for a few minutes to the equipment, to the larger pieces of equipment that your firefighting unit had during the summer and second half of 1993. Can you briefly tell the Judges, please, what fire trucks or tanks or equipment, large equipment, you had available to you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Earlier on, I mentioned that we had a command vehicle, Lada Niva. Up until June of 1992, we also had a vehicle for transporting people and equipment that was damaged through neglect of our men, and it was in this damaged state that it was brought over to our facilities. Then we had two water tanks. Their capacity was five tonnes or 5.000 litres. And then we also had Zastava 650 AM [phoen] that was a special vehicle for decontamination of tall trees and plants. It was purchased sometime in 1985. This is what we had and what was operational. However, sometime in January or in mid-February, 1993, it so happened that one of our vehicles was stolen, one of the water tanks, and we never managed to find it or to trace it. That means that we had two TAM water tank trucks and a Zastava 650. Their capacity was 4.500 litres. And we also had the command vehicle. Now, this command vehicle wasn't of much use to us unless we had to occasionally transport equipment somewhere, but other than that, we didn't use it much. As for the water tank trucks, they were owned by the firefighting association of Mostar. One of them, one of the water tank trucks of 7.000 litres, the one that we received from civilian defence staff in order to use it, it seems that when the reserve forces and members of Serb formations were there, they got it out of aluminum. And then after a while, the civilian defence staff gave it to us to use it. It was produced by factory called FAP. Its capacity was 7.000 litres. It was yellowish in colour. The colour used to be yellow, that's what I'm trying to say. So this is what we had in terms of fire trucks. Initially, our hoses were quite long. Later on, as we went out to put out fires, the hose -- hoses were damaged and were basically barely usable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me just see if I understand, sir, and correct me if I'm wrong. Based on what you've said, do I understand that there were essentially three functioning fire trucks, if we can use that terminology, that could actually be used to fight fires during this time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could I ask for the Registry's assistance that Exhibit P09220 be displayed. 9220. You will have to move down, I believe, to page 6233. Using the second -- page 14 if that assists. All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell us what is depicted or shown on Exhibit P09220.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: We can see one of the vehicles that I described produced by FAP, capacity of 7.000 litres. You can see it now in a prettier colour, and the licence plate is clear enough. At the time when we received this truck, it was anything but a firefighting truck. I think that 4 to 5.000 German marks had to be invested in order to bring it up to this condition. A lot of parts were changed on it; glass, windshield wipers, the pump, rotation lights, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Is this the vehicle, sir, that you said had previously been yellow?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please -- and perhaps you can use this photograph just to illustrate these points if it will assist you. Can you tell us how these vehicles, the trucks, were equipped in terms of lights, sirens, any signalling devices, and can you also tell the Judges, please, if they were marked in any way that would distinguish them from what might be considered a combat vehicle.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I have to tell you that everywhere in the world, including our country, fire engines are bright red. They have the colour of fire. This is sort of an unwritten rule that applies everywhere in the world, including our country. The mere fact that these vehicles are of this colour, naturally that doesn't mean that they can't be used for anything else, but I am assuring you that they were not used for anything else except for their basic purpose, to carry water to put out fire. We also had rotation lights, but there was no point in using them at the time. We had a siren that was also pointless to use at the time. And if anybody else could see some other purpose in this vehicle, then that's their opinion. I can tell you about something funny that happened with one of our water tank trucks, Zastava, which was -- its capacity was 4.500 litres. So this vehicle went, full of water, to a part of the town called Gornji Zanik. As soon as it arrived on site and starting -- and started distributing water to the population near Rudnik, a gun started firing and it pierced the water tank completely, made it look like a piece of Swiss cheese. And then the driver stood there and managed to flee to a house nearby. On the following day, we had to tow the truck back because its tyres were flat. So we had to tow it back to our premises. Then on the following day, on the radio, Postojna, we heard this piece of news announced: "Yesterday the HVO soldiers were extremely efficient. Among other things, they -- they hit a truck which had delivered fuel to the army of BH." I'm now assuring that it was our truck, that it carried water. It carried water to the civilian population. There was no way it could have carried fuel. We had an enormous shortage of fuel. We had to use fuel from a substation in order to have fuel for our vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you a question about the firefighters in your -- in your organisation. How -- how were they dressed when they were on duty? Was there a uniform; and, if so, what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. I have to tell you this: While we still had our old uniforms, which were typical ones, were identical in the entire former Yugoslavia, those were trousers with deep pockets and then shirts, and then a shirt that came over it, and then a jacket with a somewhat thicker lining. All of these pieces of uniform were dark blue. Later on, as the uniforms got damaged - we went inside the buildings which were on fire, so naturally they got damaged - and then frequently when our colleagues from abroad would come, such as Pompiers sans Frontieres, and then also firefighters from other cities abroad, they would bring us their old uniforms, but they would be of the same colour, dark blue, without any insignia. And those were the uniforms that we used. Sometimes we would also have helmets on our heads.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, can you tell the Judges, was there any resemblance between the uniforms worn by firefighters and those used by the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No, not at all. Not even resembling it. The uniform of the BH army members and BH MUP members as well as the HVO were camouflage uniforms. The BH army and the BH MUP uniforms were mostly older, and that was the only difference between them and the HVO. But at any rate, those were camouflage uniforms, and sometimes people had their own pieces of clothing that they would put on. But there was absolutely no resemblance between their uniforms and ours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, very briefly before we move on to another topic, you've made references to this, apart from these large pieces of equipment, the three fire trucks that you had, can you just briefly explain to the Judges, what did you do from May of 1993 through the remainder of that year to keep all this equipment running and operable? What did you have to do to accomplish that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's very difficult to explain this. On the whole, we tried to patch up the equipment that we had. I'll give you an example. A 15-metre firefighting pipe that is penetrated by a piece of shrapnel or a sniper shot would be patched up. We then have an eight metre pipe, for example. We'd join two such pipes together and we'd have a normal pipe, a normal hose. The greatest difficulty was when we had flat tyres. You don't have any new tyres, and you always drive around areas where there's shrapnel and where there are pieces of metal. So we -- we just had to make do and ask for individuals to lend us some glue so that we could patch up the tyres. It was very difficult to maintain the vehicles so that they could be of service.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, in moving forward, I think it would be helpful at this time, Mr. President, if indeed the -- a map of the city of Mostar, at least a large part of the city, was available. I suggest that because of the number of markings that I would expect the witness to make in the next hour or two of his testimony, it will be easier to actually do that on a hard copy rather than trying to mark it on the screen, if that's agreeable. And for everyone, the map is Exhibit P09517.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm not going to ask you -- well, I will, sir. Just to way -- just to orient everyone in the courtroom in light of some of the testimony you've given so far, can you please on that map now mark or show us where the -- your fire station, your fire headquarters, was located during this period of approximately May until the end of 1993.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'd just like to point out that this map is a very small one. It's difficult to point out everything of interest here, but I'll try to use it to give you an idea, at least a partial idea of the locations of the events. If you can follow me, this is Marsala Tita Street in the immediate vicinity of Mazoljice. And then below you have the street of Mladen Balorda. Near the Marsala Tita Street there was Coko Rila's [phoen] house at this corner. We were below this house. Opposite there was the Razvitak department store.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I would like you to mark where the firefighting headquarters was located, and if you would put a number 1 at that location, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I've marked the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Since you just mentioned it and it will be coming up, I believe, shortly, can you just mark also, perhaps with a number -- with a number 2, the Razvitak building.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was right opposite our building. I'll mark this with number 2. I've done it now. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And if I could ask you to mark one additional location for now and then we'll come back to this map in a few minutes -- well, shortly. Can you also mark where what you referred to as the war hospital, where the war hospital was located. And if you see that, would you mark that with a number 3.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it quite clearly. It's right here, between number 1 and the words Marsala Tita. It's in this area between the letters M and T. I'll mark the site with number 3. And roughly speaking, this was the location of the war military hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. And so just by way of clarity in purposes -- before we go forward - excuse me - location number 1 is the firefighting headquarters, location number 2 is the Razvitak building, and location number 3 is the war hospital; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, we'll keep that map handy, but I have some other questions for you. During the year 1993, starting from approximately the 9th of May, can you tell the Judges, based on any records or information you kept, approximately how many fires you responded to in East Mostar during that time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: If you're talking about the period that started in January, before the conflict broke out on the 9th of May, well, I think that up until the 9th of May, but I'm not quite sure of the figure, but I think we dealt with between 86 and 87 fires. From May onwards -- or, from January to December, we dealt with 386 fires. About 280 from May to the end of December. But don't take this as a precise figure since a lot of time has passed since then and I don't have any precise figures, but I think that that would be the approximate number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Based on your experience at the time, sir, what caused these fires or the majority of them?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to speak frankly: Most of the fires, a large number of the fires, or almost 99 per cent of them were the result of military action. Incendiary ammunition was used or shells were fired, and this resulted in fires. There were some accidental fires for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, or tell the Judges based on your experience, observation at the time, what you saw in terms of the locations that were shelled or fired on during this time, whether they -- whether you saw anything about the targeting that was consistent or patterned, or what can you tell the Judges about that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I don't know whether there was a pattern of any kind or not, but what all these fires had in common was that 99 per cent of them had been caused by military action. So 99 per cent of these fires were deliberately provoked, since incendiary ammunition was used. If you shell the town, then it's quite obvious that this will result in fires around the town. That's quite normal. Since this is the subject that we're now discussing, I have to point out that in a large number of cases we were at risk when putting fires out, because while we gradually managed to put a fire out, we were at risk of being hit by fire. So we could have had 14 wounded, perhaps 15 killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I am going to come to that specifically, Mr. Pejanovic, in a bit. In terms of the shelling, can you tell the Judges were there any particular locations in East Mostar, based on your experience, that were targeted or shelled more than others?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. The fire station and the surrounding area, the area surrounding the Razvitak department store, as well as the military [Realtime transcript read in error "military police"] hospital. Similarly, a building where the command was located for a while. And there was a prison there for a while too. This was the public auditing building, the former public auditing building. It is now a bank. And these were the buildings that were more frequently targeted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, in the transcript it says at one point, it's written as "the military police hospital." Were you referring, sir, to what you described earlier as the war hospital?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not aware of a military police hospital. I'm aware of a war hospital where all those wounded were treated. All the wounded had the same rights there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, based on your experience, what you observed in terms of the positions around Mostar from which the shelling was taking place, the firing positions, to the extent that you saw them or come to understand where they were located?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one technical objection to the question. It's rather compound. I would rather have it broken down, because it -- there's a difference between observing something and coming to learn about it. So if we can have a clear record. I didn't object earlier when -- when something, whether it was targeted or whether it was hit, but I do object to this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. We're not getting interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was telling Mr. Scott to try and put neutral questions, although I believe that this debate is a futile one.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's apology. The microphone wasn't working and is still not working.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. I agree with that comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... tell about what you know about firing locations; that is, positions from where the firing was taking place that you've told us about in the last few minutes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I try to answer the questions put to me, but if you asked anyone, any citizen of Mostar, anyone out of the 55.000 citizens on the left bank, they would have been able to provide you with a very clear answer. This could be seen with the naked eye. There were positions on the Hum hill to the south of the town. There were positions to the west.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me stop you. If you allow me, sir, let's take it in pieces, if you will. You've just mentioned --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated] ... no longer hear the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Testing. Can you hear me now? Can you hear me now, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I heard an interpreter say that there was a bug.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are we back on, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you would look at the map again, the one you've already made the three marks on, can you indicate on the map - and I realise it may be off the map - but just indicate the general area. If it's off the map, point an arrow pointing to the general direction of the location that you just indicated, you said the firing position on Hum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we could have the ELMO back on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll repeat this. If any citizen at the time, or even today, was asked where the positions were, it would be easy to reply. One of the positions was to the south of the centre of the town on the Hum hill. There was another position west of the centre of the town, and the third position was to the north of the centre. There were a number of positions on Hum hill, on Brkanovo hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'm sorry, sir, let's work with the map a bit. Can we draw back from the map so we can see larger picture? Is it possible? Zoom out, so to speak, please. Well, let's start with that. Perhaps that's -- if you can, sir, let's start with the position you indicated. You said there was a position on the west -- on a hill to the west or a location to the west. Could you identify that by whatever name or terminology you want to use, and also mark that on the map with the letter A, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can we please have the assistance of the video booth to show -- if the picture can be scrolled down so we can see the part of the map that the witness is referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, can you do the best you can, please, to mark that location, the location -- the firing location you described as being to the west, and put a letter A on that location or an arrow toward that location.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I said that the map was a small one, but I will try to use it. Brkanovo hill is about here, above the words "Siroki Brijeg." I'll mark it with the letter A.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think we could show a proper picture. We have dozens of map and either another map should be put here, because this is a schematic map, and we are here now entering the area of a military -- discussing military positions. We should have adequate map. This one could be useful for what the witness did so far, like some locations in the city will do, but now we are -- we are going into entirely another area of -- of issues. That is at least my suggestion. We will not get the picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I believe that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: -- the witness can give us a general idea of the locations by using this map, which this same map can then be used for the particular locations in the town of Mostar. I'm not asking him to mark with great precision at this point. I'm asking him to give -- advise the Chamber of the approximate locations or directions from the firing positions that he was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. But that is exactly what my dear colleague said: Approximate. Approximate this and approximate that, and then later somebody will say, well, the HVO had a position over just here, and it is approximate. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It is approximate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: -- it is approximate. With a military map, it would be precise, or it wouldn't be shown at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be happy if Mr. Kovacic wants to ask cross-examination questions on this. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Let the witness tell us in which direction this hill is to be found, the hill to the west.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I've already said, it's about here, above the words "Siroki Brijeg." This is how I have to explain it. I can't explain it in any other way. A little further away there's the second position, where you have TV transmitters now. It's part of the Mikuljaca hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, would you please mark -- would you put a marking on that and would you make that B.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, a moment ago, sir, you made reference to a location that was north of the town of Mostar. Can you please scan the map and again give us an indication of that location.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's to the north of the centre, in this area between Rudnik and Rastani. It's in the Raska Gora area. It's difficult to point out the location precisely but I'm trying to give you an approximate idea of where the positions were located.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Would you please mark that with a C or, again, an arrow, indicating the approximate location of that place with a letter C.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And, sir, you've indicated several times a position on Mount Hum. Can you show the Judges, please, the reference -- the location in reference to Mount Hum, and could you mark that with the letter D.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the position to the south of the centre. It's a dominant position in the town itself, so it's visible regardless of where you're standing, regardless of your position, viewpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right, sir. Moving away from the map for a moment, I would like to ask you questions in terms of the shelling and damage that was done to locations in Mostar during 1992, 1993, can you tell us first of all, was there any damage or destruction of Serb Orthodox churches in 1992?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There's no doubt that there was a church that was hit in July. There was the cathedral church. It was set on fire in mid-July, and then it was blown up. It was -- it was a church, and the old church was subsequently set on fire. Fortunately, it wasn't blown up. It was only set on fire. It was recently renovated, and I think it's now functioning normally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: When you said, sir, mid-July, what year were you referring to in reference to the destruction of the church?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: In 1992. I apologise. In 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us, sir, if you know, who or what organisation blew up this church that was, as you said, blown up?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is what I learnt from others. I really don't know who was responsible for the act. If I knew, I'd provide you with the names. I wouldn't hesitate. But at the time, they said that the HOS forces had set the church on fire, the Croatian armed forces. And a while ago, a citizen told me that he had footage of the mining of the church. He said he would provide me with them. But we met at a meeting, and he mentioned the fact that I'd be provided with footage or photographs showing who had actually blown the church up. It was suggested in the conversation that we had that perhaps HVO soldiers did that, who had been aided by elements from the Croatian army. I can't say that this is certain, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you about mosques, and I'm -- again I'm talking about 1992, we're going to come to 1993 in just one minute. Can you tell us, please, of any information you have about any mosque being destroyed in Mostar in 1992? Destroyed or damaged, substantially damaged.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, because, as I said, on the 11th of May I went home, that means I had to pass by Karajzibegova mosque, I saw that the minaret of the -- the tower of the mosque had been affected. I saw that that mosque had been destroyed. Part of the tower, part of the minaret had been destroyed and half of the mosque had been destroyed. I don't know about the other mosques, I'm not aware of them having been destroyed. 20

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm going to direct your attention specifically to 1993. Can you tell the Judges, please, to your knowledge how many mosques in East Mostar -- I'll come to West Mostar in a moment. Can you tell the Judges how many mosques in East Mostar were destroyed or seriously damaged in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: In East Mostar, if we say -- if we say that Karajzibegova mosque had serious damage inflicted to it and then Lipova mosque and then Nemed Pasina Dzamija [phoen] was partially damaged, and then the mosque in Mahala, and finally Sarica mosque; all of them had partial damage. I say "partial" because in some cases it was the minaret was destroyed and some of them, in addition to that, had also holes through the dome.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, you've said -- or we've said so far and the question that's put to you was destroyed or damaged. Based on your knowledge and observation, how was -- what was the -- what was the way or the manner in which these mosques were destroyed or damaged? By what activity or conduct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I think I can say, based on personal observation, that the damage was caused by shelling, and these had to be shells of higher calibre because an ordinary gun would not have been able to produce such damage. So -- so it had to be artillery pieces that inflicted this damage. And sometimes the shells would pierce the dome and exit through the other end, sometimes they would destroy the dome, and many minarets were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Sir, going back to the map that you were working with previously, could you please take the marker and mark the locations of the mosques in East Mostar that you understand were destroyed or damaged in 1993. I'm not going to ask you to name -- to write on the map the name of each one for now, but if you could just mark the locations of the mosques that you've told us about in the last few minutes in East Mostar.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: We have Karajzibegova mosque, here at the crossing of two streets.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters didn't hear the names of the streets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm sorry. For the interpretation, could you please state again the name of the streets, the street references that you gave? Just now for the location.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: So at the corner of Brace Fejzica Street and Karajzibegova Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to ask you to mark mosque -- I'm going to ask you to mark those just for now with an X just so we can distinguish those from other markings that you've made and will make on the map. If you can just mark anything that's a mosque with an X, please. Can you go on to the next one, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This has been done already. The next mosque is not far from, as one goes through Marsala Tita Street and descends down to the market, it is somewhere here, where the letter B is. You see this word "Brankovac" written, and this mosque is called Under Linden Tree, or Podlipa, mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again would you mark that with an X, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: The next mosque is lower down, below the letter X, not far from the 1st of May Square, Koski Mehmed-pasa mosque. And it's located between the Neretva River and the road leading to the old bridge. Here. I marked it here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. It may assist the Judges, perhaps, in reference to the old bridge, or the Stari Most, as a point of reference, can you just mark on the old bridge -- where on the map is the old bridge or Stari Most?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Not far from the letter X. Not far from this letter --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps you can --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: -- further to the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Perhaps you can give the bridge number 4.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Right here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you continue on on the mosque, please, the next mosque.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Right upon the place where you descend from the old bridge, under this word "Grad," there was the Esnafa [phoen] mosque. Earlier there was a leather manufacturing workshop here, and this is where members of this trade association had their own mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Continue on, please, if there are more. If you've come to the end, say so, but otherwise would you please mark the next mosque.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. Not far from the steps leading down to the old bridge, there was, and there still is today, the so-called Inat [phoen] mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate street reference in reference to that mosque just so we have another reference in the record, please, if possible?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's in the street called Marsala Tita Street, but it's further in from the street, some 30 metres inside from the street. And it's to the left, to the south, of the old bridge. It is a very visible building. One cannot miss it. If one went down Marsala Tita Street, one had to pass this mosque. Then further on in Mahala, in Gojka Vukovica Street, there is a mosque somewhere halfway between the space in this inscription, Gojka Vukovica Street. It's basically across from this word "Luka." I'm giving you approximate locations, just approximate locations for mosques, where they used to be. Then across from this place we have Sarica mosque, which is right here in this portion of Marsala Tita Street. From the word "Luka" there's a street running called Podharem, and somewhere in that area, in this triangle, this is where Sarica mosque would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And does that complete all the mosques you would like to mark on -- in East Mostar that were destroyed or damaged in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I apologise. I still owe you another mosque. This is the mosque at Musala. It was below us, below our premises, our fire brigade premises. It was below Cietiste [phoen], Srejca and Mladen Balorda Street. I marked it with a letter X. So this is the last mosque on the left bank in this group of mosques that used to exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you then, directing your attention to West Mostar, and can you tell the Judges anything you know about the mosques that were destroyed or severely damaged during 1993 in West Mostar. And again, can you give us a marking with an X.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: But prior to that, please allow me to say this: I heard that these mosques were destroyed. Three mosques and a mesjid located in Ilici, as far as I know -- as far as I know, but I'm not sure. I think that mesjid in Ilici has been renovated. I know that the mosque at Banovci was also renovated and also the mosque at Podhum. The third mosque destroyed -- and all three of them were razed to the ground; there was grass growing there. So the third mosque was somewhere near the first elementary school in Podhum. It still stands in ruins nowadays. There is nothing left, basically. I will try to find it on the map.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And which one -- can you again give us some street reference or something for the record for that particular mark, the one you've just made, sir.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Right here, this part where the mosque at Podhum was destroyed. I think it's still called Podhum, unless they changed the name. Then the next mosque was located at the corner of Franjevacka Street [phoen] And Queen Katarina Street. It was on the corner here, and it was not renovated. It was not rebuilt. And then the next mosque was in the area called Balinovac. Right around here, if you can follow where this word "Balinovac" is, it's near letter B. And here, I marked it here. So this mosque in Balinovac and the one in Podhum, these two have been renovated since. And the one at the corner of Franjevacka and Queen Katarina Street has not been renovated. And as for the mesjid in Ilinovici [phoen], it has also been renovated. I can't show you this mesjid on the map, it's further up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you explain for the record, sir, when you refer to "mesjid," what a mesjid?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's actually also a mosque but one without a minaret.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The mosque that you've just shown us the last few minutes in East Mostar that were damaged or destroyed in 1993, do you know what party or organisation was responsible for destroying or damaging those mosques?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's really hard to say right now, because anybody could have manned the artillery pieces. What is certain, though, is that the fire launched from the western side, from western part of the town, is what caused the damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, one last location, sir. Can you tell the Judges about any other Muslim site or religious site that you know about that was targeted in 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Other than these mosques that I marked on the map, I don't know for any others except the old bridge, unless that's what you mean. And I wouldn't link this with Bosniaks. This is a bridge built in the Turkish times, and this bridge is a symbol of the town, whether people like it or not. It will remain a symbol forever. Perhaps this is precisely why it was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me ask you not on the bridge, the old bridge for a moment, but was there a location near Blagaj that you're aware of that was targeted?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Blagaj, yes, but that's something different. That's true. In July, I established a forward fire brigade in Blagaj the day I was appointed commander of the fire unit. I learned on the basis of information available to me that it was necessary to establish at least one fire unit in Blagaj, and we did that. Blagaj itself, just like our town, did not have enough resources. So -- so we devised this arrangement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, if you let me --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is to say --

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Just in the interests of time, please. I'm sorry to interrupt you. Could I direct your attention specifically to the targeting of a location in Blagaj that you're aware of, and could you tell the Judges, please, specifically about that.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to clarify how that came about, but I will be brief. Twice, on two occasions, Pompiers sans Frontieres came to visit us. They were from France. So they came once, and the other time firefighters from Swansea, in England, came to visit us. We wanted to show them some interesting sites in the area, so we took them to the source of the Buna river, and we showed them the location called Tekija. As we were travelling back, twice the multi-barrelled rocket launchers -- this is something that people explained to me later on because I'm not much of an expert when it comes to artillery -- but at any rate, these Chinese-made multi-barrelled rocket launchers launched missiles that literally flew above our heads, and they hit the area to the left of the source of the Buna river and Tekija itself. Tekija is an oriental Islamic religious facility, and for over 25 years the gatherings of various Dervishes is organised there. This is a pilgrimage site for them. Fortunately, the missiles didn't make a direct hit. Rather, they hit a piece of rock above Tekija, and then some of the stones tumbled down, hitting the roof of Tekija.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before Mr. Karnavas intervenes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Karnavas, be brief please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes. I've looked at the documents that were provided to us by the Prosecution, and I could be in error, but I don't see anything that was provided to us from the Prosecution regarding these events that are being mentioned at the moment. It's not in the proofing notes. Perhaps I'm mistaken, but I certainly would like an explanation from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. What happened in Blagaj, is it mentioned in the indictment or in the pre-trial brief?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This particular incident concerning Tekija -- let me just double-check. Not specifically -- not specifically charged in the indictment. The witness told us about this after he came to The Hague as one of the particular items that he was aware of in connection with religious properties, and he talked about the mosque, and in connection were telling us about the mosque, he told us the story about -- the information about this location Tekija.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. President, yesterday afternoon I was provided with what is titled as "Supplemental Disclosure Statement of Witness Ratko Pejanovic," the gentleman here. Perhaps it's an oversight that this was not mentioned, but it certainly is not on the one page, what we normally call proofing notes, and obviously had we had this, we would have been able to at least be aware of the situation. I would hope that this would not happen again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. This was a matter of context?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And I have one other question about it and then we're finished on the topic, and I believe it will be time for the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, when you said you saw the -- or made reference to these Chinese-made multiple rocket launchers that were fired over your head, can you tell the Judges from what warring party, from what organisation these missiles were fired toward the Tekija complex?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, as I said to you, I heard from people in Blagaj that these were Chinese-made missiles. I don't know about that for a fact. But definitely the missiles were launched from the HVO positions, which were located somewhere in the area called Hodbine, in that main area.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And you witnessed these missiles impacting the area of Tekija yourself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Clearly so, because missiles flew above our heads. Literally, they zoomed above our heads, and we got really scared. We started running because we were afraid that new missiles would be launched and that there would be a stray missile or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Pejanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I suggest that would be a place to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, we shall now make a break so that you can have a rest and something to eat. We shall resume around 1.00. --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.24 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, several times in your testimony today so far you've also referred to the delivery of water in East Mostar, and I'd like for the next few minutes to ask you some questions about that, and I'd like to divide up my questions to you, please, in two parts. First, can you tell us what the delivery -- or the water system was in connection with East Mostar during the period roughly 1992 up until but not continuing after May 1993. Can you just describe that time for us, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me give you a brief sentence as an introduction. The situation was very bad with water supply. While the conflicts were raging between the Serbs on one side and Bosniaks and Croats on the other, all bridges in town were destroyed. Why am I saying this, that the bridges were destroyed? Not because the bridges were destroyed, but because main roads, main channels of the water supply system went through the bridges, which meant that, once the bridges were destroyed, the left bank was cut off from that system. There were no roads and no water supply. The only thing remaining -- or, rather, the only bridge remaining was the old bridge, which had one piece damaged during the conflict with the Serbs. Then the Serbs withdrew from the city and bypasses were constructed. So on the opposite bank, on the right bank, these bypasses linked up the water system to main water pipes. Three bridges, Sarinski bridge, Lucki bridge, and Tito's bridge had these bypasses whereby the citizens were able to get water and where we were also able to tank water and then transport it and distribute it to other residents. This is how it was until the 9th of May, 1993, when new conflicts and bypasses were cut off or disrupted and there was no more water supply to the left bank. I don't know who or what we should thank for this, but in two locations -- and I suppose that the reason for this was the fact that the valves, the main capital valves, were not in order and were not able -- they could not be shut off completely. So as a result of that, we had constant water supply at two locations. There wasn't a lot of water, the supply was not an immense one, but enough to fill some containers. One of these two locations was in Sevnica [phoen] near the court building. There was a subterranean hydrant there. Then they started targeting us. This was at the intersection of two streets. We then moved to the courtyard of ElectroHerzegovina, the electrical utility company. There was also a subterranean hydrant there, and we were able to use it for a long period of time. When I say "long period of time," I mean about two months. And this lasted all the way up until the metal bridge erected by UNPROFOR forces instead of Tito's bridge. This was the bridge that linked the left and the right bank and enabled us to go to that part of the town to fill our tanks and supply drinking water for residents and also water we needed to put out fires. So after the bridges were destroyed and these supply lines also destroyed, there was still some water supplied to the area -- rather, to the buildings which belonged to the Bulevar. There was a hydrant there, and there was enough water to fill, for example, a cup or a small container or a bucket.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, sorry. Let me stop you there because you've given us a lot of information. Let me go back and address a couple of things. And I think again I think it would be helpful to use the map. So if I can ask you, please, to look at the same map we were looking at before lunch, which, for the record, is Exhibit P09517. And focusing now on the time after May -- after the 9th of May, 1993. If I heard you correctly, in the last few minutes you said there were two hydrants that remained at least partly in operation or flowing on the west side of the river. And could you mark -- could you mark those. Could you show us first the first hydrant. I'm going to ask you to mark that W1, for water 1, for no other reason. If you can show us the first location, please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's take it in order. The first location where we filled containers with water is once you cross the Tito's bridge and then turn left. In the first street there is a street called Adema Ilidza, and then there's a road there leading to the Bulevar, and the court building is right across. So right here, on the corner where the letter A is, this is where that hydrant was, the subterranean hydrant in the street. The second hydrant was somewhat further up. It was in the yard of Electroprivreda, the electric utility company. Right here in this area where it says "Adema," where you see the text "Adema," right there there's a privately owned building. First there's the court building, then a passage and a privately owned building, and right next to it is the electric utility company building, and in their backyard there was a second hydrant that we used until the bridge was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So mark that with --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I will mark it with W2.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: All done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Now, if I understood your testimony a moment ago correctly, to access those two locations, W1 and W2, by truck, you obviously had to cross the river via a bridge; correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, certainly. We had to go over the bridge on the Neretva, which was erected between the two conflicts. It was a metal bridge erected by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you circle that bridge as it then existed and let's just call that B1 for bridge 1.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was here, where it says Titov Most, or Tito's Bridge. I will put a rectangle around it, and I will put an arrow. And what letter do you want me to use?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: B1, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Please.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please repeat? Do you want me to put B1?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Yes, please, B1.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now, how long after the 9th of May, 1993, was that bridge available to you, or when did that bridge -- when was that bridge destroyed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I have to say, frankly, that I don't know the exact date, but I think that it was after the second part of July. And thereafter, one couldn't cross that bridge any longer. It was still possible for pedestrians to cross, because some planks had been placed, and they were able to cross to the street Adema Buca, where the forces of BH army were.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Tell us, please, after the bridge was destroyed, what were the sources of water to the people in East Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: These two hydrants that I mentioned, for us on the left bank, were no longer acceptable. The one that was in Adema Buca Street was only available to the local residents. In parallel, as I told you, civilian authorities were being established, and they were among the first one to establish a professional fire brigade, which was the one that we belonged to. And they also established a water utility company. Later that became a publicly owned company. So they took over the water supply from that moment on, and it was only up to us to distribute that water. In addition to that, there was another supply of water. It is somewhat unexplainable, but once again I think that due to a bad valve, from this part of town where the old bridge was, there in the vicinity of the old bridge, there was a hydrant. As soon as you crossed under -- crossed the bridge under the Cardak building, there was a hydrant. It had even been shelled. It was hit by a shell. Then once at night I went to replace that hydrant, to repair it, after it was shelled. So we constructed a bypass with plastic pipes, and then we went to the left bank immediately there. As soon as you cross the bridge, to the part called Bijuka [phoen]. So it was some 30 to 40 metres from the bridge, not more than that. We created a pedestal there with five or six faucets. We provided water pressure through our fire hose.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. Mr. Pejanovic, this is on the east side of the bridge, on the east side of the river, this pedestal?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. On the east side, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Continue.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: So we had these six faucets that residents could go to for 24 hours, although it was a bit more risky to go there during daytime. And people would come with various containers, whatever they had. I was among them. And sometimes during night-time I would transport 300 to 400 litres of water when my wife wanted to do the laundry. And we also used that water for drinking, cooking, and everything else. And the water available to the firemen was solely the water coming from the Neretva River. There was a fire hydrant pumping water from the Neretva River through the pipes to Naca Street [phoen], where water was then poured into other containers. This site was targeted and fired upon several times. From the northern part of the city, they shelled the city of Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Once again, you've given us quite a bit of information. You've said -- let me go back with a couple of questions. You've said that going to this -- what I think you referred to as a pedestal, this water outlet with about six faucets, you said going to that site to collect water was risky. Could you please explain to the Judges why it was risky to go to that location.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. This area was shelled by mortars several times, and in several instances people were wounded. Fortunately, nobody was killed, but, yes, people were injured there. In Mostar at that point in time, there was a prohibition on movement -- rather, there was a curfew, and the time for curfew was changed in the period of 24 hours. I'm sorry that I didn't bring any documents with me - because I have them - documents showing that we firemen had permits to move throughout the town throughout 24 hours, whether we were working or were on leave or anything else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. Pejanovic, before I forget, can I ask you to please put a W3 -- excuse me, a W3 by that third water location near the old bridge.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: As I said, it was right by the old bridge. I know that part of the city very well. There's a flat area and then there is a cascade of five or six steps leading towards that pedestal, and I will put W3 there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: All done.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Now -- thank you. Right before I interrupted you, for which I apologise, you were making reference to filling your trucks with water for firefighting purposes. But before we come to that, let's just make sure in terms of drinking water supply, in the second half of 1993, apart from the three locations you've indicated, were there any other drinking water sources for the people in East Mostar other than the ones you've marked so far?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. As I said to you, all we had is the water that came, I suppose due to a bad valve. And then there was water from the Neretva River. The water that was poured into water trucks was chlorified. Depending on the amount of water in the system, a certain amount of chlorine was added, and this water had the colour of blood. It was red. Forty-five to 50 minutes were needed for the chlorine to evaporate so that the water would only after that be available for drinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sorry. Was there particular location -- that was my next question: Was there a particular location along the river where the water was removed from the Neretva for the purpose of putting in the tanks and treating the water with chlorine as drinking water? Was there a particular location on this map where the water was collected?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, I can give you an approximate location. It's a bit hard, but it was here. There is the Tito's bridge and then there's another bridge. Not a proper bridge, rather a makeshift bridge for logistics support. And to the south of that makeshift bridge, on the bank of the Neretva, there was a pump, pumping water from the river and pumping it up to Fejzica Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Could you show us where the pump was located, approximately, and mark it W4.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let me just orient myself. So here, where you have near the Tito's bridge, this makeshift bridge, this passage. Close to that makeshift bridge there's one passage, and then the red area, and then -- rather, in this narrow red or pink area, which denotes probably a facility of some kind, so approximately there, there was a pump pumping water from the river, and pumping it up to Fejica Street. This is where we tanked water. I have to say that this system functioned only at certain intervals, because there wasn't enough fuel and this pump was operated by petrol. So during a day, we would be able to tank water four or five times, depending on the situation. And sometimes, if we had fires which went on for a long time, then pursuant to an authorisation of the city government, this pump would be left working longer, and water was then available only to us. Nobody else could use this water. Once we started distributing water to people, to residents, and then we received information that a fire broke out somewhere, so we immediately stopped distributing water to people and then went to intervene to put out the fire. That was our primary duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Can I ask you, please, to put a W5 at the location -- if I understand your testimony, W4 is where the pump itself was located, but you seemed to indicate that the water was then moved by pipeline to another location where it was actually collected in the truck, if I understand you. So can you mark the other collection point, the other end of that system, if you will, with a W5.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I have to digress. W4 marks precisely the location of a water truck when they tanked water. If you want, I can mark with a W5 the location where the pump was when it was pumping water. It was right there on the riverbank, and I will mark it with W5.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is where the water was pumped, and then through the pipes it was transported to Fejica Street, and this is where we tanked water into our trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And again, sir, just so the record is clear, with this additional testimony in the last few minutes, have you now shown us to the best of your knowledge all the sources of drinking water for the people in East Mostar in the second half of 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Anybody can confirm this. I'm not the only one who knows this. Any resident can tell you where water pumps were. There were simply no other ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, during 1993, were there any efforts by the HVO side to interrupt or stop the flow of water from any of these sources?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Whether there were any attempts to disrupt the water supply through this valve or through the pipes that went over the old bridge, I don't know that, but the fact is that there was constant water supply through that system. And I suppose that it was because some of the valves was not functioning properly, and they were not able to shut off water supply. This is why there still was some water in the pipes. As for tanking water from the Neretva, or pumping water from the Neretva, in view of the configuration of the Neretva bank in that area, the simplest thing for us would have been to pump water through our water tanks, because there were no limitations to doing that. However, due to the configuration of the banks, we simply had no access. We couldn't approach the river with our trucks. Therefore, the only remaining possibility was this pump in Djuro Salaj area. So that was the only location where we were able to tank water. It was widely known. It was no secret. And this area was targeted dozens of sometimes, and our vehicles were damaged there dozens of times too. The windshield -- windshields were damaged, the body of our water trucks, tyres were also damaged. People were injured sometimes, too. Fortunately, nobody was ever killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Was there at any time during 1993 a flood on the Neretva river that interfered with the flow of water, drinking water?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is also one of the unfortunate things. The left side broke down, and once it was broken down, the water from the accumulation lake rushed down the river, and it was very noisy. Before the water reached us, we could hear the noise of an enormous quantity of water rushing down. As I told you, we had a pump pumping water from the river, and when this huge amount of water reached it, fortunately it only turned the pump upside down and knocked it on a rock which was there. People from the water utility company - and this was in December - they undressed down to their bathing suits -- I'm trying to remember the name of one of these men. He jumped into the river, dived in, found the location where the pump was. We figured that the pump did not float away because it was very heavy. So he had some rope, and he was able to tie the pump with the rope. And all of this was taking place in the morning hours, until 11.00 or 12.00 noon. In the afternoon hours, they started cleaning the motor of the pump and also its parts, and the pump was operational again sometime at around 7.00 in the evening and was able to pump water and supply it to the residents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Are you aware, sir, of what caused the flood that knocked the pump out, at least momentarily, at least for some time?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: The only explanation is that the shut-off valve was -- was opened. For a while, after the Washington Agreement, the shut-off valve was not operational; destroyed, mined. I think that some kind of a water missile destroyed it, a torpedo, something like that. This is my assumption. I have nothing to support this. But the fact is that after the Washington Agreement was signed and there was a cease-fire, this shut-off valve for a long time was not operational until the dam was reconstructed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Not going as far in time as the Washington agreement, but if I direct your attention back to December of 1993, was there a time that the dam on the Neretva River north of Mostar was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. I said a moment ago that it happened in December when the pump fell into the river. And Torlo Miron was the name of the man who dived into the river. He now works at the University of Mostar. Before, he was an employee of the waterworks company, utility company. He was the man who dived into the river, located the pump on the riverbed, dived again a second time, tied the rope to the pump, and managed to extract it. It was December. I can't be exact about the very day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Do you know who destroyed the dam?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I would prefer to say that I know who did not, because they were members of the HVO who were there in that portion where that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Pejanovic, I would like to turn to more specifically on the topic of sniping. You've mentioned before that you've written a book about some of your experiences in Mostar; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And what is the name of that book?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: The book is called "Flames Above Mostar."

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And did you discuss in that book a number of sniping incidents that took place during 1993?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to ask you, and may I be allowed to add that I wrote this about sniper incidents in 1992. So that it's not just one-sided. And in the book that I wrote, I emphasise that the first victim among the fire brigade was a close associate of mine, a very good young man, an exceptionally good young man. He was Feijzlic Camin [phoen] and he was our first victim and he fell victim to a Serb sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: So your accounts of the sniping in Mostar started in 1992, and then how long, over what period of time did you cover that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the most part I think I dealt with 1992, a few months of 1992, or it would be better to say that I dealt with the period up until the 11th of May, 1992, which was how long we were there, near the supermarket, department store. So from that point towards the Bristol Hotel in the space of a few days, well, I can't give you an exact figure, but I think about seven persons were killed precisely because they were running across Tito's bridge towards Brsol [phoen]. And one of our members too was killed at Tito's bridge coming back from a fire that had broken out the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Sir, is one of the incidents that you know about the killing of a man named Uzeir Jugo? And forgive me if I mispronounce the first name; Uzeir Jugo.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you said his name perfectly. Unfortunately, I said, God willing, this will be the last victim. He was killed just a little while after the truce was signed in 1994, the cease-fire between the Bosniaks and Croats. I was present, together with another colleague of mine, Dzemal Barakovic, and the late Jugo Uzeir, who was the driver on duty that day. And before that unfortunate hour, together with his colleague Dzemal Barakovic, saw to the tyres, pumped up the tyres, repaired the tyres. As I said, a truce had already been signed, so a little time after the signing of this cease-fire, this incident -- excessive incident took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. I'm -- now, looking back, before we go to one other piece of information. So on the map that we were looking at earlier today, you've already previously marked that, the location of the fire brigade. I don't think we have to look at it again now, but the fire brigade station was number 1 and the Razvitak building was number 2. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, with the assistance of the technical team, we are going to show now a -- basically, it's a 360-degree photograph taken from this -- the location where Mr. Jugo was killed, and then I'll ask the witness to show -- to identify certain locations in the photograph. If we can do that, please. This is exhibit -- forgive me, it's Exhibit P09139. First we'll do a full scope -- and I'll tell this for the witness's sake too: We'll do a full view, a 360-degree view, and then I'll come back to the beginning and ask the witness to identify several locations. Okay. Can we stop there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry to interrupt, but if I'm not wrong, the witness said on -- when this story started, that this poor man was killed after Washington Agreement. And if I'm not wrong, the indictment -- time frame in the indictment is from September, 1991, until the Washington Agreement. So it very well may be that we are now discussing an incident which was obviously out of the time frame. Nevertheless, since I took -- this is just one more information. There were different incidents after the Washington Agreement in entire Bosnia-Herzegovina, so if we accept to discuss this event or incident, then probably we will discuss many of them. I'm just trying to -- to show that perhaps we don't need that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll be happy to assist Mr. Kovacic. It is charged in the indictment. It is specific incident number 14 in the annex to paragraph 114 of the amended indictment. So if you have a paragraph -- if you go to paragraph 114 and to the annex in reference to that paragraph and you look at incident number 14, that is the incident charged. And the period of the indictment continues well into March 1994, to be exact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I am aware of that citation, but that is exactly my point: Is out of the frame of indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It's in the indictment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But indictment does provide the frame, the time frame. So you have to change the indictment. It is then not up to the Washington Agreement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, in paragraph 114, in annex -- in the annex, you will find -- find the list of the victims, and the last name mentioned is Uzeir Jugo, a driver of a red firefighter truck, was hit in the chest on the 2nd of March, 1994. Witness, when you talk about the death of Mr. Jugo in your book, when was he killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that it was just after the signing. Now, what the exact date is, I can now see that you said the 2nd -- I think it was the end of January or the beginning of February when the signing took place, whereas this incident quite certainly happened after the signing of the agreement, because I remember we began walking about normally, normally taking around water. We weren't as afraid of being shelled after that. So I'm quite sure about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in your book, could you tell us on what day this firefighter was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At any rate, Your Honour, not me, but there is a record in the civilian protection, because they were duty-bound to report anyone wounded and dead to the civilian protection organisation. He was hit one day and expired the following day.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the certificate concerning the death of this individual is Exhibit P07998, which indicates that Mr. Jugo was killed on the 1st of March, 1994, which is in the exhibit that you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Scott, you have to be very accurate. If you have the death certificate which is on the 1st of May, why did you state that it was on the 2nd of May?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I'll look at the indictment, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: March. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: It was March. I think we just had an interpreter's correction, Your Honour. We're talking about March of 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour. We are about to use the evidence in order to define, in order to find out whether this incident is within or without of the scope or time frame of the indictment, then I have to tell the following: First, the exhibit that my dear colleague referred to is not yet tendered, is not yet admitted. So we don't know. Second, the only evidence we have up to this moment is the testimony of this gentleman, and this witness, during our discussions, clearly said that he's sure that this person was -- that this person died after the agreements, the Washington Agreements. Yes, the truth is he also mixed up a little bit the time, he's not sure about, but he's certain it was after the time of the Washington Agreement. And the -- and that's it. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the Judges will deliberate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, before you do --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Before -- this is -- with all respect to Mr. Kovacic, this is -- this is not even a close point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that the Judges will deliberate in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: All right. Your Honour, when we argue this, or we submit further, if you look at paragraph 15, paragraph 115 and other parts of the indictment, you'll see that the indictment extends on its face until the April of 1994, has no connection to the date of the signing of the Washington Agreement whatsoever. So, Mr. Kovacic, I'm afraid, with all respect, is just simply mistaken about the significance of that date. The indictment talks about April of 1994, specifically paragraph 110: From June, 1993, to April, 1994, East Mostar was under siege. During this time, from June -- paragraph 111: During this time from June, 1993, to April, 1994, there was continued fighting, shelling, sniping. In paragraph 114, paragraph 115, it's in the annex to the indictment. Paragraph 117: The East Mostar siege ended around the 12th of April, 1994. The incident is charged in the indictment specifically, and it's within the time period covered by the indictment specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: If we can go back to the 360-degree photo, please. Now, if you can continue -- now, Mr. Pejanovic, if you can focus, please, now on the photograph as it's moving, and I would like for you to -- when you see the Razvitak building, can you please stop and tell us when you see that building.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Go back a bit, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Stop. That is the place, the location where the cistern was. From the post that you can see, or the edge of the wall, whichever you like, the corner of the wall, it was a metre and a half away, plus the width of the vehicle, so that it was on the very edge of the pavement.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Let me -- it was translated as "cistern." I'm not sure. Perhaps that's absolutely correct. Are you talking about the location of the truck?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Water truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: And this is the water truck --

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: We're not getting any interpretation. I know what it means, but I think, for the record, we need interpretation. Can we get interpretation of the witness's answer, please?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We did not hear the witness's answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: This is the location, sir, where you saw that the water truck was located at the time Mr. Jugo was killed?

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. And can you continue the photograph and identify to us anything else, like the fire station or the Razvitak building.

utterances.speaker: RATKO PEJANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the fire brigade where the water truck was standing. It was, as I say, from the wall perhaps a metre and a half away from the wall, plus its own width, which meant that it was right up against the edge of the pavement. And my colleague Mr. Uzeir worked there repairing the tyres, pumping up the tyres, patching them up. He did a bit of work on the engine together with Djamakovic [phoen]. Sometime towards the end of work I told a female colleague of ours who was in the office to make us some coffee, and while I was saying that to her, I went outside, I stepped outside, and the two of them who were standing round the vehicle started putting the equipment in order, taking away the pump and so on, and Uzeir turned round, and as you're looking at the photograph now where you can see the automobile parts poster, he passed by along the left-hand side to the pavement to put away the equipment they had been using to do the work. I was opposite the vehicle myself, and Dzemo Barakovic was up in front, in front of the vehicle, in front of the water truck. At one point in time I hear the door shut, and I saw him say, "Oh, God, oh, mother." And Dzemo Barakovic, who was in a better position because I was opposite, said to me -- it was all a split second, happened in a split second -- he said, "Uzeir has been hit." I ducked under the truck and saw him. I saw the knee -- his knee and his left elbow. He was resting on it to try and pull himself up. I have to say that at that point in time he was wearing the uniform of the civilian protection, light blue in colour. He had a wind cheater on as well. We managed to take him across our building on a stretcher to the ambulance that came straight away. We transported him to hospital. That was between half past one and fifteen to two. The next day, at that same time he died. And he had been given six blood transfusions by that time. This caused a bit of a problem. It was a zero positive blood group. We had to get that blood group in, and that gave us a bit of a problem. But it was at this same time that he actually expired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why would you like to take the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] May I ask one question? Because of the ballistic analysis, subsequent ballistic analysis, it would be very important for us if the witness were to indicate the exact spot where the person hit fell. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
